title: Gajanana Avatar — From Greed Toward Expansive Love

sections.title: Reading the Puranic Story as a Teaching of Principles
content: Recalling the context of this series of discourses on Ganesha Tattva, Latha Mahendra gives importance to the Mudgala Purana and to the efforts of Ganesha Yogendra Maharaj who made it accessible to all. She suggests that one should not stop at merely viewing the names, forms, and events in the Puranic stories as wonders, but should examine the message they carry relating to the human interior. She explains that the same Ganesha Tattva being narrated through various avatars also serves as a means to understand the different tendencies within us.

Rather than remaining stuck in the discussion of which deity is greater by comparing one form with another, the discourse states that it is important to grasp the principle being taught through that form. Using the example of an actor who assumes different roles, it is explained that even though forms change, the consciousness that is their basis can be recognized.

sections.title: Nirguna and Saguna — Two Perspectives of the Same Principle
content: The speaker explains that the Nirguna principle, which is described as being without form, name, and attributes, is worshipped in Saguna forms so that it becomes understandable to the devotee. Ganapati is not merely a specific image; the intention is that through that form a universal principle can be brought closer to the mind. In this background, while also referring to the ideas in the Ganesha Upanishad, the perspective of seeing Ganapati as the principle underlying creation, sustenance, and dissolution is conveyed.

Even in our lives, the same person performs many roles. With the analogy that differences between roles do not mean the person's inner nature is different, she suggests that the diversity of Ganapati avatars should be understood in the same way. The message that stands primarily here is that devotion should not remain limited only to the form, but should lead to the expansive consciousness that the form indicates.

sections.title: The Entry of Greed in the Gajanana Story
content: Explaining the story related to the Gajanana avatar, the speaker describes how the tendency of Lobhasura grows. What appears initially as a desire, if it does not stop even after being fulfilled, leads to more desires. She explains that lack of contentment even after obtaining power, wealth, and authority is the characteristic of greed. Referring to stages in the story such as the guidance of Shukracharya, worship, and obtaining boons, she reminds that the most important question is in which direction we use the power we have obtained.

She says that the asura in the Purana is not merely a character existing somewhere outside, but can also be seen as the form of selfish thoughts within us. If the urge to accumulate beyond necessity grows, the joys and sorrows of others may cease to be visible. This story reminds us that there is then a danger that even the power obtained through sadhana may be used not for the expansive good but for personal dominance.

sections.title: When Craving Joins Greed
content: The mind running toward another desire as soon as one desire is fulfilled is a commonly experienced matter. In the discourse, the joining of craving (trishna) with greed is specially discussed. Here, craving means not the natural effort to fulfill a need, but the endless thirst that no matter how much comes it is never enough. She explains that the cycle of wanting one more after acquiring one, and wanting more recognition after reaching one level, constantly turns the mind outward.

If this cycle is not observed, happiness always depends on some future achievement. The capacity to enjoy what is already present diminishes. The discourse suggests that while greed limits us, gratitude expands our vision. The practical idea that appears here is that rather than suppressing craving, it is important to see its movement with awareness.

sections.title: From Envy Toward Mudita
content: Referring to situations such as feeling that we too should have what others have, and the mind becoming disturbed by others' success, the nature of envy is explained. She says that at the root of envy there may be the narrow feeling that 'priority should come only to me.' Grasping the Ganapati principle means recognizing that narrow feeling and going beyond it.

In contrast, the speaker introduces the feeling called Mudita. Mudita is being able to truly rejoice when good happens to another. It is explained that when others' happiness does not appear as competition to us, and we too become partners in that joy, love expands. The message that the small circle of 'my people' can expand from the family to society, to other beings, and to the universe is important in this part.

sections.title: The Name Gajanana — A Pointer Beyond Form
content: Latha Mahendra says that the name Gajanana should not be seen only with the external meaning of elephant face. When speaking about the principle that existed before creation, if one holds only to the physical form and questions, the essential meaning may not be reached. The spiritual pointer conveyed through name and form should be examined; both the literal meaning and the symbolic meaning should be given their appropriate place.

She reminds that in the commentarial tradition there is an inner meaning for every aspect of the Ganapati form. However, they are not explanations about physical structure; they are symbolic teachings related to the mind, consciousness, and sadhana. Seen in that way, the name Gajanana becomes a means to awaken an expansive vision within us.

sections.title: The Mouse Vehicle — Symbol of the Restless Mind
content: The discourse also specially discusses Ganapati's vehicle, the mouse. Showing analogies with the mouse's characteristics of hiding things and nibbling them away, she explains that the mind too runs after many things without our knowing. She asks us to observe how small attractions snatch away our attention, time, and peace.

Ganapati being seated on the vehicle is not hating those tendencies; she presents it as a metaphor indicating the state of being able to guide them with awareness. Observing where the mind is running, and bringing it back to a meaningful resolve, become part of the practice.

sections.title: Karma, Resolve, and Self-Examination
content: The speaker examines the relationship between desires, actions, and their results from the perspective of karma. She says that rather than immediately giving a simple judgment as to why some experiences are arising, one should examine one's own responses. Instead of remaining stuck only in remembering the past and suffering, what matters is with what kind of resolve we are living now.

This teaching suggests that through practices such as meditation, self-study, gratitude, and rejoicing in the joy of others, one can journey from greed toward expansive love. When the Gajanana story is concluded, the principal question that remains is: is the restlessness that we need more increasing, or is the expansiveness of sharing what we have increasing?
